newsitem.title: UK: BoE's George warns of dispute with Germany, France.
newsitem.headline: BoE's George warns of dispute with Germany, France.

text.p: Bank of England governor Eddie George warned in an interview published on Monday that a dispute between Britain, Germany and France could threaten cooperation over preparations for a single European currency.

He told the Financial Times that a row over access to the future Target system, which will control real-time payments between banks, could cause a split between countries joining European economic and monetary union (EMU) and those chosing to stay out.

In his first public statement on Target, he called the dispute trivial in itself but added: "For the first time something was being introduced into the EMU discussion which was discriminatory for a non-monetary reason.
"We are not in the business of compromise over Target -- we are talking about principle," he said.
George stressed the need for constructive co-operation between European central banks in the European Monetary Institute, the future central bank for Europe.
France and Germany, the leading proponents of monetary union, have insisted that countries not joining EMU should face restrictions in using the Target system.

"I don't see why the situation should develop into a split between the ins and the outs. But you could see that developing if the ins felt they were imposing on themselves a discipline which is not going to apply to the others."

The EMU project faces substantial political opposition in Britain, particularly from the right wing of the ruling Conservative Party which insists the government must refuse to join a single currency when it is launched in 1999.
However, George said monetary union could be "an absolutely huge opportunity" for the City of London, Europe's biggest financial market.
"I think the potential pluses are very considerable in relation to the potential minuses."
That depended, he said, on London being ready for EMU and that EU preparatory talks remained constructive.
"I don't think there is a loss of leverage for the UK at the moment. If you have a valid point to make, everyone has been prepared to listen to it," he said.
